## One chain, highest band first

```cpp
if (score < 0 || score > 100)
    std::cout << "invalid\n";
else if (score >= 70)
    std::cout << "distinction\n";
else if (score >= 60)
    std::cout << "merit\n";
else if (score >= 40)
    std::cout << "pass\n";
else
    std::cout << "fail\n";
```

## Why the order is the whole problem

Each test only needs its **lower** bound, because `else` guarantees everything
above it was already false. By the time control reaches `score >= 60`, the
score is known to be under 70 — so `>= 60` really does mean "60 to 69", even
though nothing in that line says 69.

Reverse the chain and it collapses:

```cpp
if (score >= 40)       std::cout << "pass\n";        // 73 lands here
else if (score >= 60)  std::cout << "merit\n";       // unreachable
else if (score >= 70)  std::cout << "distinction\n"; // unreachable
```

Every score of 40 or more prints `pass`, and the last two branches can never
run. The compiler will not warn you: the code is perfectly well formed and
simply means something else.

## Four ifs is a different program

```cpp
if (score >= 70) std::cout << "distinction\n";
if (score >= 60) std::cout << "merit\n";          // also true for 73
if (score >= 40) std::cout << "pass\n";           // also true for 73
```

A score of 73 prints three lines, because nothing stops the second test from
running after the first succeeded. `else` is what makes the alternatives
exclusive — that is its entire job.

## The boundaries

The hidden cases are every edge, because this is where the mistakes live:

| Input | Band | Why it is a test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `100` | distinction | the top of the valid range |
| `70` | distinction | `>=` not `>` |
| `69` | merit | one below a boundary |
| `60` | merit | `>=` again |
| `39` | fail | the band with no lower test |
| `0` | fail | the bottom of the valid range |
| `101`, `-1` | invalid | one step outside, both directions |

Every one of those is a different answer, and a single `>` where you wanted
`>=` breaks exactly one of them. That is why testing the boundaries beats
testing the middle: `73` passes under half a dozen wrong implementations.

## Validating first

Checking `score < 0 || score > 100` **before** the bands means the rest of the
chain can assume a sane value. Doing it last would mean every other test had to
guard against a negative number, and the chain would stop being readable.

The general shape is worth keeping: **reject the impossible, then handle the
possible.** It is the same instinct as checking a pointer before dereferencing
it, or a length before indexing.
